column2: What does an ordinary SQL Server view expose without storing a separate copy of the result rows?
column3:
A virtual table defined by a query.
A normal view stores its definition rather than a copy of the result rows. SQL Server uses the definition when a caller queries the view.
Review source

column2: How does a view simplify a frequently reused join?
column3:
It hides the join behind a reusable table-like interface.
For example, define the customer-to-order join once. Reports can then query that named result rather than duplicating the join conditions.
CREATE VIEW dbo.CustomerOrders
AS
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, o.OrderID
FROM dbo.Customers AS c
JOIN dbo.Orders AS o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID;
Review source

column2: Why put a shared calculation, such as order categorization, in a view?
column3:
To define the calculation once for all callers.
Give the calculated field a stable name such as OrderSize. Every caller can use that field without repeating the underlying CASE expression.
CREATE VIEW dbo.OrderSizes
AS
SELECT OrderID,
       CASE WHEN TotalAmount < 100 THEN 'Small'
            ELSE 'Other' END AS OrderSize
FROM dbo.Orders;
Review source

column2: Which part of a view definition limits the rows that it exposes?
column3:
Its WHERE clause.
WHERE controls which rows qualify. For example, IsActive = 1 hides inactive customers without removing them from the base table.
CREATE VIEW dbo.ActiveCustomers
AS
SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName
FROM dbo.Customers
WHERE IsActive = 1
WITH CHECK OPTION;
Review source

column2: Which part of a view definition controls the columns that it exposes?
column3:
Its SELECT list.
The SELECT list names the returned fields. A report that needs employee names can use a view whose column list omits salary.
CREATE VIEW dbo.ActiveCustomers
AS
SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName
FROM dbo.Customers
WHERE IsActive = 1
WITH CHECK OPTION;
Review source

column2: How do you grant a reporting user access through a view without letting them read its base tables directly?
column3:
Grant SELECT on the view and restrict direct access to its base tables.
Grant access to the narrow view and make sure other permissions do not allow direct reads of the source. Otherwise the view does not restrict those reads.
GRANT SELECT ON OBJECT::dbo.ActiveCustomers TO ReportUser;
Review source

column2: Why list view columns explicitly instead of using SELECT *?
column3:
To keep the exposed columns deliberate and stable.
An explicit list makes the exposed fields intentional. A source schema change does not cause a newly added column to become part of that list.
Review source

column2: Why keep a view focused on one purpose?
column3:
To make its query logic easier to understand and optimize.
Keep joins and calculations relevant to the callers that use the view. A single definition for unrelated reports can make its dependencies harder to understand.
Review source

column2: An updatable view filters to active customers. What does WITH CHECK OPTION require of rows inserted or updated through it?
column3:
Inserted or updated rows must remain visible through the view.
For example, a view filtered to active customers rejects an update through it that makes a customer inactive. The resulting row would no longer satisfy the filter.
CREATE VIEW dbo.ActiveCustomers
AS
SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName
FROM dbo.Customers
WHERE IsActive = 1
WITH CHECK OPTION;
Review source

column2: Which write path can ignore WITH CHECK OPTION on a filtered view?
column3:
Modifications made directly to its base tables.
A direct write bypasses the view filter. Use a table constraint instead when the rule must apply to every eligible write path.
CREATE VIEW dbo.ActiveCustomers
AS
SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName
FROM dbo.Customers
WHERE IsActive = 1
WITH CHECK OPTION;
Review source

column2: For an ordinary joined SQL Server view without an INSTEAD OF trigger, how many base tables can one UPDATE change?
column3:
One base table for an ordinary view, including a joined view.
In an ordinary joined view, all columns updated by that statement must map to one base table. Updatable partitioned views follow special rules.
Review source

column2: Why cannot an ordinary view directly update an output column calculated by CASE?
column3:
It does not directly reference an updatable base-table column.
A CASE expression computes a result from other values. SQL Server cannot infer which source value to set when the caller tries to change that result.
CREATE VIEW dbo.OrderSizes
AS
SELECT OrderID,
       CASE WHEN TotalAmount < 100 THEN 'Small'
            ELSE 'Other' END AS OrderSize
FROM dbo.Orders;
Review source

column2: Which type of SQL Server view physically stores its result set?
column3:
An indexed view, also called a materialized view.
The first unique clustered index stores the view result. An ordinary view still stores only its definition, and indexed-view availability depends on the platform.
Review source | Fabric Warehouse

column2: Who keeps a SQL Server indexed view's stored rows current after a write to its base tables?
column3:
SQL Server updates the indexed view as part of the data modification.
A write to a base table can change the stored view result. SQL Server maintains the index during that write instead of leaving a stale copy.
Review source

column2: Why can moving a join into a nonindexed view leave a query's performance unchanged?
column3:
Its underlying query still requires execution.
The optimizer normally expands the view into the caller's query. A shorter query in the application does not imply less work for SQL Server.
Review source

column2: Which SQL object provides reusable, parameterized query logic that returns a table?
column3:
A table-valued function.
A TVF can accept inputs such as a customer ID and still supply rows to FROM. A standard view cannot declare those parameters.
Review source

column2: Which SQL object fits a callable workflow that validates input and changes several tables in a transaction?
column3:
A stored procedure.
A procedure can validate inputs, coordinate multiple writes, and manage a transaction. A view exposes query results and is not a general workflow.
Review source

column2: How do you query an existing SQL Server view?
column3:
Reference its name in a SELECT statement's FROM clause.
Use FROM followed by the view's schema-qualified name. Add an outer WHERE clause if the caller needs a smaller subset.
SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName
FROM dbo.ActiveCustomers
ORDER BY CustomerName;
Review source
